question: Should the Goddess be worshipped in the right-hand (dakṣiṇa) mode, or is the left-hand/Kaula (vāma) mode with the five tattvas higher?

sides.position: The seven modes rise from Veda to Kaula; Vāma is higher than Dakṣiṇa and Kaula highest of all (Kulārṇava 2.7-8); in the Kula dharma enjoyment itself becomes yoga (2.23-24); worship of the primordial Śakti without the five tattvas is fruitless 'like seed on rock' (Mahānirvāṇa 5.22-24).
arguments: the bliss of Brahman latent in the body is made manifest in the Kula rite (Kulārṇava 5.79-80)
the Kula scripture is Vedic in essence (Kulārṇava 2.85)

sides.position: (Kālīvilāsa) In the Kali age all classes must worship in the paśu disposition, bathing thrice daily and eating no meat; the vīra and divya dispositions do not exist in this age (Kālīvilāsa 4.2-3).
arguments: each disposition belongs to its age (6.10-16)
the great exemplars (Rāma, the Sanakas) were perfected in the paśu disposition

sides.position: (Samaya Śrīvidyā, Lakṣmīdhara) The Kaula and 'mixed' modes are to be abandoned: the sixty-four tantras aim at worldly powers, deceive even their knowers and are far from the Veda; only the inner Samaya worship is Vedic.

reconciliation.explanation: The texts themselves tie the modes to the practitioner's disposition and eligibility (bhāva, adhikāra) and provide substitutes, so right- and left-hand worship are prescribed for different practitioners.
reconciliation.detail: The Mahānirvāṇa itself restricts the tattvas and substitutes the sweet triad for householders in the Kali age (6.14; 8.170-171); the Kulārṇava restricts Kula knowledge to the tested and eligible (2.30-36; 14.9-14) and condemns misuse (5.96-105). This covers the Kaula–Dakṣiṇa difference as one of stage; it does not cover the Kālīvilāsa's denial that the vīra disposition exists at all in this age, nor the Samaya rejection of Kaula as non-Vedic.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Kaula texts hold Kaula to be the highest for all who are eligible, not merely an option; the Kālīvilāsa denies the vīra and divya dispositions in the Kali age; Lakṣmīdhara's Samaya school rejects the Kaula way outright.

question: Is Kaula practice — the Kula worship with the five tattvas, the circle and the cremation ground — a legitimate path to liberation, or a departure from dharma?

sides.position: The Kaula path is the highest (Kulārṇava 2.7-8), both enjoyment and yoga (2.23-24), Vedic in essence (2.85), misunderstood by the deluded as musk is taken for mud (2.109); the realized Kaula is beyond injunction and prohibition (9.55-58). But it is harder than a sword's edge (2.122), must be given only to the tested (2.36; 14.9-14), and is condemned when practised for pleasure: wine alone gives no perfection (2.117), the wilful and uninitiated go to hell (5.96-105), and abandoning ritual out of false learning is heresy (9.130).

(Rudrayāmala, voiced by Vasiṣṭha) The Siddhas of Mahācīna drink, eat meat and live with women 'outside the Veda' — how can perfection come without Vedic rites? The text answers through the Buddha that the Kula path begins in purity and the paśu disposition and is Vedic in its own way; the question is the orthodox objection it sets out to meet.

(Samaya Śrīvidyā) The sixty-four (Kaula) tantras beguile the world, aim at powers and are outside the Veda; the three higher classes should follow only the Vedic Samaya way (Lakṣmīdhara on Saundaryalaharī 31).
(Kālīvilāsa) In the Kali age the Kaula (vīra) disposition does not exist; worship must be pure and meatless (4.2-3).

historical_debates.name: The Vasiṣṭha–Buddha dialogue in Mahācīna (Rudrayāmala 17)
historical_debates.accounts: A narrative debate inside the text, not a recorded historical event.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Vasiṣṭha accepts the Kula way and becomes a Siddha.

reconciliation.explanation: The Kaula texts address different eligibilities (P4) and speak of freedom from injunction only for the realized, from the ultimate standpoint (P1), while binding everyone else by the samayas and warnings.
reconciliation.detail: Kulārṇava 9.55-58 ('no injunction, no prohibition') is spoken of the Kaula who has reached the goal; 5.96-105 and 9.130 bind the practitioner. This reconciles the Kaula texts with their own warnings; it does not reconcile Kaula with the Samaya and orthodox Vedic rejection of the tattvas.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Samaya Śrīvidyā and orthodox Vedic authorities reject the Kaula rites as such, not merely their misuse; the Kaula texts reject the claim that their way is non-Vedic.

question: Should blood offerings (bali) be made to the Goddess?

sides.position: (Kālikā Purāṇa) The Goddess is pleased by offerings; by them liberation and heaven are won and a king conquers his enemies; mantra-purified blood becomes nectar (67.1-12; 67.19-22). The same text restricts them: brāhmaṇas must not offer wine or certain victims, a human offering needs the king's permission, and pumpkin, sugarcane or spirits are 'equal to' a victim (67.23; 67.46-52; 67.113-117).
(Kālīvilāsa) In the Kali age worship is to be performed in the paśu disposition, with pure food and without meat (nirāmiṣa) (4.3).

(Vaiṣṇava) Killing animals is not true worship; the Bhāgavata warns that animals slain in sacrifice await their slayer in the next world (Bhāgavata 4.25.7-8, recalled), and the Goddess is Kṛṣṇa's power acting by his will (Brahmasaṃhitā 5.44); Bengal Vaiṣṇavas reject bali.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Kālikā Purāṇa enjoins what the Vaiṣṇava and paśu-bhāva positions forbid.
candidate_readings: P4-stage / adhikāra: the Kālikā Purāṇa itself grades offerings by class and permits substitutes; the substitutes (anukalpa) could be read as the tradition's own path for those who will not kill.
P7-arthavada: the promise of liberation through bali (67.5) as praise of the rite rather than doctrine of liberation.
Not reconcilable while one side holds killing to be an offering and the other a sin (ahiṃsā).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Kāmākhyā tradition holds bali to be enjoined by scripture; Vaiṣṇavas (and Jains and Buddhists) reject any reconciliation that allows killing.

notes: Related: dsp:animal-sacrifice-epic (U05). The Bhāgavata verse number is recalled, not checked.

question: Are the vīra and divya dispositions (and the five tattvas) permitted in the Kali age?

sides.position: (Kālīvilāsa) No: the divya and vīra dispositions 'do not exist, do not exist' in the Kali age; all classes worship in the paśu disposition (4.2-3); divya belonged to Satya–Tretā, vīra to Tretā–Dvāpara (6.10-16).

(Mahānirvāṇa) Yes, with restrictions: the five tattvas are proper to Śakti worship (5.22-24), the tantric path is the only one for this age (2.7-15), but in the Kali age the last tattva is only with one's own wife and householders use the sweet triad (6.14; 8.170-171).
(Kulārṇava) The Kaula is highest without any age restriction, though only for the tested and eligible (2.7-8; 2.30-36).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Kālīvilāsa denies outright what the Mahānirvāṇa and Kulārṇava allow under conditions.
candidate_readings: P4-stage: the Mahānirvāṇa's substitutes for householders show a graded permission; the Kālīvilāsa's rule may address ordinary worshippers of the four classes.
P2-standpoint: the Kālīvilāsa speaks from the standpoint of the age (cosmic), the Kulārṇava from that of the qualified individual.
Not reconcilable if the Kālīvilāsa's 'does not exist' is taken as a universal prohibition.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each text presents its own rule as Śiva's command for the Kali age.

question: Is Kṛṣṇa a form of Kālī, or is the Goddess a power of Kṛṣṇa?

sides.position: (Toḍala) The ten Mahāvidyās are the ten avatāras; 'Bhagavatī Kālī herself arose as the form of Kṛṣṇa' (10.11); Kālī is the source of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva (Nirvāṇa Tantra 10.42-43; Karpūrādistotra 12).

(Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava) Kṛṣṇa is the Lord himself ('kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam', Bhāgavata 1.3.28); Durgā is his one power of creation, maintenance and dissolution, sustaining the worlds like his shadow and acting by his will (Brahmasaṃhitā 5.44).

reconciliation.explanation: Each tradition describes the relation of Goddess and Kṛṣṇa from the standpoint of its chosen deity (iṣṭa-devatā); both agree the two are inseparable as power and power-holder.
reconciliation.detail: Jīva Gosvāmin's commentary on the Brahmasaṃhitā itself cites 'yaḥ kṛṣṇaḥ saiva durgā' and speaks of the non-difference of power and powerful; the Toḍala makes Kṛṣṇa Kālī's form. The reconciliation records complementary standpoints only.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Gauḍīya tradition rejects any subordination of Kṛṣṇa to the Goddess; the Śākta texts reject the Goddess's subordination to Kṛṣṇa. Both reject the claim that the two views are simply the same.

question: Is this world a 'frame of illusion' to be seen through, or a 'mansion of mirth' to be enjoyed in the Lord?

sides.position: (Rāmprasād) 'This world is a frame of illusion' — the mind should not be deceived by it but turn to the Mother.
(Āju Gosāi, a Vaiṣṇava contemporary, in the tradition's account) 'This world is a mansion of mirth' (majār kuṭi), where one eats, drinks and makes merry with the Lord.

historical_debates.name: Rāmprasād and Āju Gosāi's song-exchange
historical_debates.accounts: Bengali oral tradition; later cited by Ramakrishna (U52).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Remembered as a friendly contest of songs.

reconciliation.explanation: The same world is a trap to the one still bound and a mansion of mirth to the one who has realised the Lord (Mother) in it — the reading given in the Ramakrishna tradition.
reconciliation.detail: Recorded as the later tradition's reconciliation (U52 to anchor in the Kathāmṛta); both songs are quoted there.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: None recorded; the exchange is remembered as good-humoured.
